findings.title: `cf config unset --project` cannot clear the stale shared-file copy, breaking the documented collision fix path
findings.description: The design states "**Delete:** mirrors write — deletes from whichever project file the key's scope maps to", with `migrate-personal` as "the one exception that touches the *other* project file". So for the personal key `git.integration_branch`, `delete(key, 'project')` deletes from `.context-forge.local.toml` only. But line 146 tells the user to clear the stale shared-file copy with "a separate, explicit `cf config unset <key> --project`", and verification step 9 (line 259) runs exactly that command and then expects `cf check` to be clean. Under the stated routing that command instead destroys the developer's local value (the very thing the collision rules at line 146 exist to protect) and leaves the stale copy in `.context-forge.toml`, so the `personal-config-in-shared-file` warning (line 142) never clears. The same problem hits any pre-migration project: unsetting a personal key whose value lives only in the shared file is a silent no-op on the personal file while the shared value keeps resolving via the read-time fallback. This leaves the plan-required "defined migration/compat story" unmet for the collision case the design explicitly chooses to handle. Fix the design by defining a dedicated shared-file deletion path (e.g. `migrate-personal` gaining an explicit stale-copy cleanup action, or a documented raw-file edit), not by reusing `unset --project`.

findings.title: New `ConsistencyChecker` rule assumes infrastructure that does not exist and leaves its file-reading dependency unspecified
findings.description: The rule is described as "added alongside the existing config-hygiene-style checks". I read `ConsistencyChecker.ts` in full: its rules are all document-artifact consistency checks (task-vs-plan, frontmatter, review gates, stale worktree paths, frontmatter schema). There are no config-hygiene checks; the constructor's `ConfigManager` is used only for `resolveGateConfig()`. So the stated integration point is false, and the design also never says how the rule will "scan the shared project file": `readToml` is a module-private helper in `ConfigManager.ts` and is not exported by `config/index.ts` (it exports only `ConfigResult`, `ConfigListEntry`, `ConfigManager`, `getUserConfigPath`, `getProjectConfigPath`). Two plausible mechanisms exist — a new raw-TOML read helper in the introspection layer, or iterating personal keys through `config.get(key)` and checking `source === 'project'` — and the design picks neither. This leaves the success criterion "`cf check` ... reports exactly one warning-severity finding" under-specified, and quietly pushes config-file hygiene into the document-introspection layer against the project's "clear separation between components" convention. Name the read mechanism and where it lives; also note that `cf check --slice N` / `workflow_check` with `sliceIndex` use `check()` (per-slice rules), not `checkAll()`, so "both already run the full suite" is only true in all-slices mode.

findings.title: `cf init` gitignore behavior is under-specified, untested, and doesn't cover the pre-migration population the slice targets
findings.description: Three gaps: (1) "append that one line" does not define what happens when an existing `.gitignore` lacks a trailing newline — naive concatenation produces a merged pattern that ignores nothing, i.e. exactly the silent personal-config leak this slice exists to prevent. The "substring/line check" can likewise false-positive on a comment line or a negated pattern. (2) The new unit-test list (lines 221-222) covers `ConfigKeys`, `ConfigManager`, `ConsistencyChecker`, and `migrate-personal` — there is no test for the new `cf init` write, nor for the collision branch (verified only manually in step 9). That violates the architecture HLD's explicit principle "**No behavior changes without tests**" for a brand-new file-writing behavior; step 3's `cat .gitignore` is not automated coverage. (3) `init.ts` wraps all existing setup steps in `if (!opts.lite)`, while the walkthrough uses `cf init --lite` (line 233) and expects the ignore line — the design never says the new write must sit outside that guard. Most importantly, the ignore line is only ever added by `cf init`, so any project initialized before this slice (the exact population the Migration Plan at lines 138-146 is written for) never gets it: after `migrate-personal` creates `.context-forge.local.toml`, that file is untracked and unignored, so personal settings can still be committed. The repo's own `.gitignore` has `*.local`, which does not match `.context-forge.local.toml`. The stated Value ("prevents personal settings from being silently committed") is therefore unmet for existing projects. Define a coverage path for them (e.g. ensure the ignore line when the personal file is first created, or a checker finding for missing gitignore coverage) and add tests.

findings.title: Failure modes are not enumerated for the new personal-file read path
findings.description: The "Failure modes" section covers only writes: `migrate-personal`'s write-then-delete window, `set()`'s write failure, and the `cf init` append. But `get()`/`list()` now read a second TOML file on every call, which is a new I/O path, and the only statement about it is "file-not-found-means-empty semantics completely unchanged" (line 121). A malformed, permission-denied, or partially-written `.context-forge.local.toml` is not addressed: `readToml` rethrows everything except `ENOENT`, so `get()` would throw — consistent with the project's "fail explicitly" convention, but the design leaves that handling implicit rather than stated. Note also that `smol-toml` parse errors on the personal file would abort `cf config get` with no key (which calls `list()`), affecting unrelated shared keys. Add one line naming this path's failure class and its handling strategy (propagate, no silent empty-object fallback). The new message shape — `config_get`'s `configPaths` gaining a `projectPersonal` field — likewise has no stated failure/contract note, though that one is a pure additive response field.

findings.title: Design is overweight for a 3/5 slice; several mechanisms can be cut or deferred
findings.description: The plan assigns effort 3/5, risk Low–Medium, and asks for a "defined migration/compat story" — not a migration subsystem. The read-time fallback (line 140) already guarantees no regression, so the heaviest option has been chosen: a new `ConsistencyChecker` rule + a new `cf config migrate-personal` subcommand + three-branch collision semantics (absent / different / identical, line 146) + a dedicated verification step for a double-stale case that only exists because the skip branch leaves the stale copy behind (line 259). A lighter story — the fallback plus one documented manual migration procedure — meets the plan's requirement while removing two new mechanisms and their test burden; if the command is kept, the collision branch can be deferred to Future Work and `skip` replaced with a straightforward "leave shared copy, warn" behavior. Line 268 additionally invents a new requirement ("there's never a window where personal keys can silently linger") that neither the plan nor the architecture states. Also cuttable: the 9-step Verification Walkthrough (lines 231-259) largely restates the Success Criteria (lines 212-218); "Integration Points → Provides to Other Slices" (line 204) is speculative guidance about future config keys with no consumer; and "Interfaces Required" (line 49) enumerates ten callers only to say none change. None of these restatements are required by the architecture HLD.

findings.title: MCP `config_get` tool description will be stale after the precedence change
findings.description: The only MCP change listed is "surface both project config paths" (lines 34, 72, 280). But `packages/mcp-server/src/tools/configTools.ts` advertises in its tool description: "Resolution order: project config → user config → built-in default." After this slice the order is project-personal → project-shared → user → default, so the documented contract becomes wrong. The design's "Interfaces Required" section (line 49) says MCP `configTools.ts` needs no changes beyond the path addition and asserts the `.source` inspection was "verified by inspection" — accurate for the code, but it overlooks the description text. Adding that one-line description update keeps the MCP consumer contract honest and costs nothing.
